Judgment Delivered:

December 6, 2024

GRAMMOND J.

Introduction

[
1
]

The applicant Rafael Zaki (“Mr. Zaki”) seeks the
judicial review of a decision of the University Discipline Committee (“UDC”) of
the respondent University of Manitoba (the “University”).  Pursuant to the
UDC’s decision issued on May 12, 2022 (the “Decision”), Mr. Zaki was expelled
from the Max Rady College of Medicine at the University because of three Facebook
postings (the “Postings”) that he made in February 2019.

[
2
]

These reasons relate to the following preliminary
motions in this matter:

a)

the University’s motion to expunge:

(1)

two excerpts of the notice of application (the
“Application”) as filed;

(2)

the vast majority of Mr. Zaki’s first affidavit
sworn August 3, 2022 (“Affidavit #1”);

(3)

Mr. Zaki’s second affidavit sworn May 7, 2024
(“Affidavit #2”); and

(4)

Mr. Zaki’s third affidavit sworn May 7, 2024
(“Affidavit #3”);

b)

Mr. Zaki’s motion to amend the Application; and

c)

Mr. Zaki’s motion to require that the University
disclose disciplinary decisions that relate to another student.

[
3
]

Although motions to expunge affidavit evidence
are typically heard together with the substantive application to which they
relate, in this case I ordered that the University’s motion to expunge would
proceed before the hearing of the Application
[1]
.

Background

[
4
]

The Decision is the second UDC decision to
impact Mr. Zaki’s academic career with the University.  A previous UDC decision
to expel Mr. Zaki from the College of Medicine was quashed by Champagne J., in
part because the panel failed to address a reasonable apprehension of bias (
Zaki
v. University of Manitoba
,
2021 MBQB 178
).

[
5
]

The Decision at issue here arose from a
disciplinary hearing held before the UDC on April 8, 2022 (the “Hearing”),
which proceeded as a trial
de novo
,

at which both Mr. Zaki
and the University were represented by counsel.  The UDC does not record its
proceedings, so no official transcript of the Hearing is available.  The
parties agree that at outset of the Hearing, the UDC directed that no
recordings were to be made of the proceedings.

[
6
]

Affidavit #1 reflects that, despite the UDC’s
direction and his lawyer’s advice that he should not record the Hearing, Mr.
Zaki did so surreptitiously (the “Recording”).  Mr. Zaki deposed that he did
so because he “feared continued bias” by the UDC and that his words would be
twisted, or that the University would lie and not provide him a fair hearing.  A
transcript of the Recording is attached to each of Affidavit #1 and Affidavit
#2, and two electronic versions of the Recording are attached to Affidavit #2.
Mr. Zaki seeks to rely upon the Recording in support of both his motion to
amend the Application and the Application proper.

[
7
]

Mr. Zaki seeks to amend the Application by
adding an allegation that a reasonable apprehension of bias arose at the
Hearing on the basis that the Chair of the UDC panel (the “Chair”) was at the
material time a professor in the College of Pharmacy, who reported to the Dean
of the Faculty of Health Sciences (the “Dean”).  The Dean was one of the
decision-makers in Mr. Zaki’s expulsion from the College of Medicine and testified
at the Hearing.  Accordingly, Mr. Zaki takes the position that the Chair should
have recused herself from the Hearing.

[
8
]

In support of these bias allegations, Mr. Zaki
seeks to rely upon the following evidence:

a)

the Recording and the transcripts thereof, which
reflect:

(1)

the submissions of Mr. Zaki’s counsel on
recusal;

(2)

the response of the University’s counsel; and

(3)

the decision of the UDC to proceed with the
Hearing; and

b)

Affidavit #2, which reflects that at the time of
the Hearing, Mr. Zaki was unaware that the Dean oversaw both the College of
Medicine and the College of Pharmacy.  He deposed that he came to that
realization earlier this year.  Affidavit #2 also includes the documentary evidence
upon which Mr. Zaki seeks to rely regarding the relationship between the respective
positions of the Chair and the Dean.

[
9
]

I will consider first the University’s
expungement motion as it pertains to the Application, Affidavit #1, and
Affidavit #2.

Issue 1:    Should any of the Application, Affidavit #1, or
Affidavit #2 be Expunged?

[
10
]

The University’s motion to expunge is based upon several grounds:

a)

the Recording was obtained surreptitiously, and
is therefore an abuse of process;

b)

the affidavits include new evidence that was not
before the UDC; and

c)

the affidavits contain evidence that is irrelevant,
duplicative and/or argumentative.

The Law

[
11
]

Court of King’s Bench Rule 25.11(1)(c) provides that the court may
strike out or expunge all or part of a pleading or other document, with or
without leave to amend, on the ground that it is an abuse of process of the
court.

[
12
]

In
Manitoba Metis Federation Inc. v. Brian Pallister et al.
,

2019 MBQB 118
, the court considered a motion to expunge evidence on a
judicial review application.  The court noted that the onus is on the moving
party to satisfy the court that it is plain and obvious under Rule 25.11 that
the impugned evidence should be struck.  The court also noted that the party
seeking to adduce evidence that was not before the administrative
decision-maker has a corresponding onus to demonstrate that the evidence is
relevant, necessary, and falls within a recognized category of admissibility.

[
13
]

The court in
Manitoba Metis Federation Inc.
also
stated:

[66]    …judicial review is usually conducted based on the record
that was before the administrative decision-maker when it made the impugned
decision.  Evidence that was not before the decision-maker is generally not
relevant or admissible on the judicial review.  That limitation is made to
ensure that judicial review does not expand into a
de novo
hearing.

…

[68]    The courts have recognized narrow, principled exceptions to
the general inadmissibility of extrinsic evidence.  Those exceptions include
evidence to establish:

i)

that the record is incomplete or contains gaps;

ii)

procedural unfairness, jurisdictional error or
bad faith; …

[69]    …even in respect of these exceptions, if the court can
adequately assess the pleaded grounds of review based on the existing
evidentiary record, extrinsic evidence can be seen to be not required and thus,
may still be inadmissible.

…

[71]    Even where extrinsic evidence may be admissible, affidavit
evidence will nevertheless be struck or expunged if it contains:

1.  spin, advocacy or
argument;

2.  non-expert
evidence;

3.  conclusions of
fact or law; or

4.  irrelevant
statements.

[72]    The affidavit presenting what may be admissible extrinsic
evidence must be limited to the deponent’s personal knowledge of the facts or
other evidence that the deponent could provide as a witness in court. … While
such an affidavit may contain information and belief with respect to
non-contentious facts, it must nonetheless specify the source of that
information and the fact for that belief. …

[73]
Affidavits on a judicial review containing extrinsic evidence
which, by itself, is otherwise inadmissible according to a
Queen’s
Bench Rule
, or because it does not fall within any of the narrow and
principled exceptions (to the general inadmissibility of extrinsic evidence) or
because it does not otherwise properly form part of the “record”, may, depending
on its specific nature or deficiency, constitute evidence which is properly
struck on the basis of any of the grounds set out in
Queen’s Bench Rule
25.11
.

[citations omitted]

[
14
]

In
Bernard v. Canada (Revenue Agency)
,
2015 FCA 263
, the
court noted that the policy considerations underlying these rules of
admissibility relate to judicial efficiency, and the different rules that apply
to an administrative decision-maker and a reviewing court.  More specifically,
a reviewing court has limited powers and must not become a “forum for
fact-finding and on the merits of the matter”.

[
15
]

The court listed as an exception to the general rule of
inadmissibility “evidence relevant to an issue of natural justice, procedural
fairness, improper purpose or fraud that could not have been placed before the
administrative decision-maker and that does not interfere with the role of
administrative decision-maker as merits-decider”.  The court noted that the
list of exceptions to the general rule is not closed.

[
16
]

The court added:

[26]    …if the
evidence [was] available at the time of the administrative proceedings, the
aggrieved party would have to object and adduce the evidence supporting the
objection before the administrative decision-maker.  Where the party could
reasonably be taken to have had the capacity to object before the
administrative decision-maker and does not do so, the objection cannot be made
later on judicial review.

The Recording

[
17
]

I will consider first the admissibility of the Recording.

[
18
]

In
Spiring v. Gould
,
2008 MBQB 282
, the court
considered a situation where a litigant ignored the direction of a Master to
file a motion for production of documents, and instead issued a subpoena to
obtain the production of the disputed documents.  The court stated that “[t]o
permit the respondent to ignore the Master’s binding directions would bring the
administration of justice into disrepute and make a mockery or the court
process and rules” (at para. 21).

[
19
]

In
Prouse v. Lands Appeal Board
,
2015 SKQB 66
, the
court considered an appeal from an administrative tribunal where the applicant
had made a surreptitious recording of the hearing.  The court stated:

[39]    …surreptitious
recording of proceedings at this Lands Appeal Board hearing or any other
hearing ought not to be encouraged and ought to be specifically discouraged.
The appellants in this case have their remedy in the event the Lands Appeal
Board refused to allow the recording and the parties thought the recording to
be necessary in the circumstances.  They may apply to the court.  Instead of
exercising a remedy within the system or discussing the matter with those
involved, the appellants took it upon themselves to record the proceedings.

[
20
]

Prouse
is the only authority before
me involving the surreptitious recording of an administrative proceeding, and
it is not binding upon me.  Other case authorities involved the admission into
evidence of surreptitious recordings taken in employment
[2]
, commercial
[3]
, or family
[4]
law contexts, where the courts
have applied the general rules of evidence and considered relevance, necessity,
the application of any exclusionary rules, and whether the probative value of
the recording was outweighed by its prejudicial effect.

[
21
]

In
Hennessey v. Canada
,
2016 FCA 180
, the court stated
that allegations of procedural unfairness cannot be raised on judicial review
if they could reasonably have been the subject of timely objection in the
first-instance forum.  More specifically, the court stated “[a] party must
object when it is aware of a procedural problem in the first-instance forum.
It must give the first-instance decision-maker a chance to address the matter
before any harm is done, to try to repair any harm or to explain itself.”

Analysis

[
22
]

The University’s written Student Discipline
Appeal Procedure provides:

2.72    If the appeal hearing is in closed session, no observers may
be present in the room.  If the appeal hearing is in open session, any
observers present will not be allowed to contribute in any way to the
proceedings.  Regardless of open or closed status, no electronic or other
recording devices will be permitted.

[
23
]

The University argued that
Prouse
should apply in this
case, in the context of a quasi-judicial proceeding involving opposing parties,
because litigants need to conduct themselves in accordance with directions and
rulings of courts and tribunals, to uphold the administration of justice and
integrity of the justice system.  Cases involving a recording made as between
two private parties who were not bound by rules of procedure are not relevant.

[
24
]

Mr. Zaki submitted that the use of the Recording is so intertwined
with the future assessment of the Application on its merits that it cannot be
plain and obvious that the Recording should be struck at this stage.  More
specifically, there are a variety of areas in which the Decision is at odds
with the oral evidence presented at the Hearing, and without the Recording he
cannot establish what was said at the Hearing.

[
25
]

Mr. Zaki also contended that
Prouse
is an “outlier
decision” that is not binding in Manitoba, has never been followed by any
court, and is distinguishable on its facts, because in
Prouse
the
recording was of poor quality and was incomplete, and there was no pre-existing
concern that the administrative tribunal was biased.

[
26
]

Mr. Zaki argued that if he had asked the UDC to record the Hearing, his
request would have been denied pursuant to section 2.72 set out above, which does
not give the UDC discretion to order that the Hearing be recorded.  He also
argued that he could not have sought a judicial review of that denial because
to do so would have been premature.  As such, he argued that he had no “right way”
to obtain a recording and transcript of the Hearing, unlike the parties in
Prouse
.

[
27
]

I have considered Mr. Zaki’s motives for making the Recording, and from
a practical perspective, I understand why he wanted the Hearing to be
recorded:  based upon past experiences and the failure to address a reasonable
apprehension of bias after his first expulsion, he did not trust the UDC.  Having
said that, the decision of Champagne J. did not entitle Mr. Zaki to ignore the Student
Discipline Appeal Procedure, or to pick and choose which aspects of the administrative
framework he would follow at the Hearing.

[
28
]

Leaving aside whether there was merit to his mistrust of the UDC
prior to the Hearing, if Mr. Zaki wanted the Hearing to be recorded, he should
have sought the UDC’s agreement to do so in advance thereof, regardless of his belief
that his request would be denied.  He certainly appears to have planned to make
the Recording prior to the Hearing, because he discussed doing so with his
counsel who advised against it, wisely.  As such, there appears to be no reason
why a request to record could not have been made of the UDC before the Hearing.

[
29
]

The law is clear that judges have an inherent and residual
discretion to prevent an abuse of the court’s process and to maintain its
integrity.  The “concept of abuse of process was described at common law as
proceedings that are “unfair to the point that they are contrary to the
interest of justice”…”
[5]
.
In addition, abuse of process is a flexible concept that applies in many
different contexts
[6]
.
More particularly, “[r]ather than focus on the motive or status of the parties,
the doctrine of abuse of process concentrates on the integrity of the
adjudicative process” (
Toronto
).

[
30
]

I agree with the court in
Prouse
that the
surreptitious recording of proceedings, including those before an
administrative tribunal, ought not to be encouraged, and ought to be
specifically discouraged.  As stated in
Spiring
, courts have
procedural rules
that apply to many different
aspects of the proceedings before them, and it is of the

utmost importance to the administration of
justice that those rules be respected and followed by parties, including parties
that believe they have been wronged.  This statement applies equally to
administrative tribunals.  To find otherwise would undermine the framework upon
which the administration of justice depends, and in this case would have the
effect of retroactively changing the terms upon which the Hearing proceeded.

[
31
]

The reality is that for a variety of policy reasons, many
administrative tribunals do not record the proceedings before them, such that
no hearing transcript is available on a judicial review application.  In this
case, by all appearances, everyone involved in the Hearing, except Mr. Zaki, agreed
to proceed in that manner.

[
32
]

By seeking to rely upon the Recording in the Application, Mr. Zaki
is attempting to enhance his position after unilaterally changing the parameters
of the Hearing, a quasi-judicial proceeding.  In the interests of justice, I
will not permit him to seek forgiveness for the Recording after failing to seek
permission to make it.  In other words, to allow Mr. Zaki to rely upon the
Recording as evidence on the Application would make a mockery of the UDC’s
process, rules, and directions, and would violate the fundamental principles of
justice, which I will not countenance.

[
33
]

In addition, the usefulness of the Recording and the transcripts are
at issue.  In
Christie Building Holding Company, Limited v. Shelter
Canadian Properties Limited
,
2021 MBQB 77
, the court stated “it does
suspend disbelief to suggest optimistically that a court reporter could now
accurately transcribe… a hearing that they did not attend in order to
reconstruct a transcript that is destined to become part of a record that is
still potentially incomplete”.  In this case, it appears that Mr. Zaki’s
counsel engaged a court reporter to transcribe the Recording, but the transcript
does not identify all of the speakers on the Recording and there are different
versions of the Recording and the transcript before the court.  These factors detract
from the probative value of the Recording and transcript.

[
34
]

I have considered
Law Society of Saskatchewan v. Abrametz
,

2022 SCC 29
, where the court discussed the remedies to be imposed for an abuse
of process, and more particularly whether the continuation of a proceeding
would result in more harm to the public interest than would a stay of proceedings,
which is granted only in the clearest of cases.  To apply those principles to
this case I have balanced the usefulness of the Recording on the Application against
the egregious manner in which it was obtained, and I have concluded that the abuse
of process outweighs the benefits of admitting the Recording into evidence.  The
abuse of process was significant, and it is plain and obvious that the
Recording should be expunged from the court record.

[
35
]

For the foregoing reasons, the Recording, the transcripts, and all
references thereto shall be expunged from the Application, Affidavit #1, and Affidavit
#2.

[
36
]

Having made these findings, I need not consider the University’s argument
that creating the Recording and filing the transcripts constituted a collateral
attack on the prohibition of recordings at the Hearing.

[
37
]

If I am wrong that it is plain and obvious that the Recording ought
to be struck as an abuse of process, I have also considered the admissibility
of the Recording as extrinsic evidence, with regard to the framework set out in

Manitoba Metis Federation Inc.
and
Bernard
.  Mr.
Zaki argued that the Recording is both relevant and necessary to the
Application, and should be admitted as context and background, pursuant to the
procedural fairness exception to the exclusionary rule.

[
38
]

It is clear that the Recording is relevant to the Application,
because in the Application Mr. Zaki has:

a)

sought a declaration that the Decision is
unreasonable because the UDC failed to properly consider or give any weight to new
evidence critical to the Decision, including the oral evidence given at the
Hearing; and

b)

alleged that the UDC’s version of what occurred
at the Hearing, as demonstrated in the Decision, is not in keeping with the
content of the Recording, especially on the crucial elements of the Decision.

[
39
]

As such, when the Application is heard, the court must assess the
UDC’s consideration of the evidence presented at the Hearing.  I accept that
the Recording could be of benefit and fill a gap in the record (subject to an
assessment of weight), because without it the court would not have direct
evidence of what was said at the Hearing.

[
40
]

I note also that the Recording is not evidence that could have been
put before the UDC.  On the contrary, it is evidence of what unfolded at the
Hearing.  As such, the Recording is not the type of extrinsic evidence that is
typically considered on a judicial review application.

[
41
]

Having said that, in
Bernard
at para.
28
, the court
stated that the list of exceptions to the rule against admitting extrinsic
evidence is not closed.  The court cited an example of a reviewing court that
received evidence of the submissions of counsel before an administrative
decision-marker, which were not otherwise on the record with the reviewing
court.  The court in
Bernard

stated that “[t]he reviewing court
admitted evidence… so that it could assess whether the decision was
unreasonable.”  In another example cited, a partial transcript prepared by one
of the parties was admitted because the reviewing court was satisfied that it
was reliable, did not work on unfairness or prejudice, and was necessary to
allow it to review the administrative decision.

[
42
]

As such, the Recording is the type of extrinsic evidence that can be
admitted on a judicial review application, if it would facilitate the reviewing
task and would not invade the UDC’s role as fact-finder and merits-decider.

[
43
]

I have also considered whether the Recording is necessary.

[
44
]

Mr. Zaki argued that the Recording is necessary to show that the
Decision reflects conclusions and inferences that did not properly arise from
the evidence at the Hearing, and to establish bias.  More specifically, he
submitted that there was no evidence before the UDC that he was insincere in
his expressions of remorse or that he did not appreciate his professionalism
obligations.  As such, the Decision was unreasonable and for the UDC to have concluded
as it did, it must have been biased against him.

[
45
]

Mr. Zaki argued that the written submissions to which the University
has pointed on this motion are legal submissions relating to the application of

The
Apology Act
, C.C.S.M. c. A98,

and are not evidence.
He also noted that his only opportunity to respond to the University’s written
submissions was during his oral evidence at the Hearing.

[
46
]

Mr. Zaki also pointed to three specific excerpts of the Recording
that he says are not otherwise on the court record on the Application:

a)

the statement by the University’s counsel that
the “Faculty” did not consider suspending Mr. Zaki;

b)

the statement by the University’s counsel that
if Mr. Zaki had demonstrated sufficient insight into the matters discussed in his
apologies, the Postings would have been forgiven; and

c)

Mr. Zaki’s alternative submission that the UDC
should impose a one-year suspension as time served.

[
47
]

The University argued that the court can assess the issues related
to Mr. Zaki’s sincerity and appreciation of his professional obligations on the
basis of the written record, without the Recording, because there was ample
evidence in Mr. Zaki’s written submissions that supported the UDC’s findings.  The
University also noted that Champagne J. was able to comment upon the
reasonableness of the first UDC decision without the benefit of a hearing transcript.

[
48
]

For the reasons that follow, I have concluded that the Recording is
not necessary to the Application, and should not be admitted as extrinsic
evidence.

[
49
]

The Recording is not the
only
potential source of evidence of
what was said at the Hearing.  Multiple individuals, including Mr. Zaki, were
present at the Hearing and could have attested to what was said in the
proceedings, based upon their respective recollections and/or notes that they
may have made at the material time.  I appreciate that an individual’s
recollections and/or their notes could be seen as less reliable than would a
recording of the same event, but having said that, a person’s recollections
ought not be discounted automatically.

[
50
]

In other words, to the extent that Mr. Zaki seeks to allege that the
Decision does not reflect accurately what was said at the Hearing, he could
have deposed to his own recollections of what was said, and perhaps other
individuals in attendance could have done the same.  I will assume that this
evidence would have been met with opposition from the University on the basis
that it would be potentially unreliable extrinsic evidence, but had that
approach been taken those issues could have been adjudicated on their merits,
and Mr. Zaki would have avoided the finding that his choice to make the
Recording constituted an abuse of process.

[
51
]

I have also considered the extent to which the Recording can assist
the court to determine whether the Decision reflects conclusions and inferences
that did not properly arise from the evidence.  One of the UDC’s tasks at the
Hearing was to assess Mr. Zaki’s sincerity and appreciation of certain issues
relating to professionalism, and the Decision reflects a variety of comments
and conclusions about Mr. Zaki’s actions, statements, and progress leading up
to and at the Hearing, including with respect to consistency, context, his professional
growth, and his willingness to take responsibility for his actions.

[
52
]

Mr. Zaki can argue on the Application that the UDC made findings of
fact in the absence of evidence, or contrary to the evidence before it, which
the court will consider when assessing the reasonableness of the Decision, but
I reject Mr. Zaki’s submission that the Recording is necessary because his oral
evidence at the Hearing was determinative of the issues of his sincerity and appreciation
of his professional obligations.  In fact, Mr. Zaki’s oral evidence at the
Hearing was
one
component of the overall record before the UDC, and
should have been considered in that context.  Whether the UDC’s consideration
of Mr. Zaki’s oral evidence was adequate or “paltry”, as Mr. Zaki contends, can
be considered on the Application without the benefit of the Recording.

[
53
]

In other words, the absence of the Recording will not render the
court unable to properly dispose of the issues raised at the hearing of the
Application, because the court will be tasked with reviewing the reasonableness
of the Decision, for which the details of the evidence may not be necessary.
In
Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v.

Vavilov
,

2019 SCC 65
, the court stated that formal reasons for an administrative
decision will not always be necessary, and the corollary thereof is that a
basic record of proceedings will generally suffice on a judicial review
application.  Moreover, when the court hears the Application, it will not be
permitted to find facts or draw its own conclusions arising from either the
oral evidence specifically or the evidentiary record generally, including with
respect to Mr. Zaki’s sincerity or appreciation of his professional
obligations.  If the court did so, the Application would be converted to a
hearing
de novo
, and the function of the UDC would be usurped.

[
54
]

In conclusion, the Recording is not necessary and should not be
admitted as extrinsic evidence on the Application.

Conclusion on the Recording

[
55
]

The Recording, the transcripts, and all references thereto
[7]
shall be expunged from the
Application, Affidavit #1, and Affidavit #2, without leave to amend, including:

a)

Affidavit #1:

(1)

the last sentence of paragraph 76;

(2)

paragraphs 77, 78, and 79;

(3)

the following phrase in paragraph 80: “I believe
that these hearing materials are important because”;

(4)

paragraphs 81 and 82;

(5)

paragraph 89, save and except for the first two
lines thereof, ending with “impact on others”;

(6)

paragraph 90;

(7)

the phrase “[t]he hearing materials also
demonstrate” in paragraph 91;

(8)

the phrase “and I believe that the hearing
materials demonstrate this.” in paragraph 92.

(9)

paragraph 95; and

(10)

Exhibit “E”;

b)

the Application:

(1)

paragraph 14; and

(2)

the final phrase of paragraph 15 beginning with
“as demonstrated …”; and

c)

Affidavit #2:

(1)

paragraph 4, save and except for the phrase beginning
“…in August 2022 …” and ending “ultimately reported to Dr. Postl ….”;

(2)

paragraphs 5, 23, and 24; and

(3)

Exhibits “B”, “N”, and “O”.

Issue 2:    Should the Abner Report be expunged from Affidavit
#1?

[
56
]

Attached to Affidavit #1 is a report dated June 10, 2022 prepared by
Dr. Erika Abner regarding Mr. Zaki’s completion of ethics and professionalism
instruction through the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Manitoba (the
“CPSM”) over nine sessions, from October 2021 to May 2022.

[
57
]

The University seeks to expunge from Affidavit #1 those paragraphs
that relate to the Abner Report, together with the report itself.  The
University argued that the report is new evidence that was not on the record
before the UDC, and post-dates the Hearing.  As such, to add the Abner Report
to the record on the Application would make this court a fact-finder, which is
not its role.  Moreover, the UDC had before it some evidence of Dr. Abner’s
work with Mr. Zaki, and it is not unusual for additional information to arise
after a hearing.

[
58
]

Mr. Zaki argued that the admission of the Abner report would fill a
gap in the record, because the UDC concluded that there was a lack of progress
in Mr. Zaki’s remediation through the CPSM.  The UDC also found that the Abner
remediation process would not succeed because Mr. Zaki had no insight into his
wrongdoing, and that speculation proved to be wrong because he completed the
instruction and did well.

The Law

[
59
]

The general rule against the admission of extrinsic evidence on a
judicial review application is set out above.  A judicial review is not a
de
novo
hearing at which the parties are generally permitted to enhance the
record of proceedings.

Analysis

[
60
]

It is clear that the UDC was aware that Mr. Zaki was undergoing
remediation instruction through the CPSM, and that Mr. Zaki testified about his
progress in that instruction at the Hearing.  The Abner report reflects that as
of the date of the Hearing, Mr. Zaki had completed 6 of 9 sessions with Dr.
Abner.  For reasons unknown, the UDC did not have evidence before it
from
Dr. Abner
of Mr. Zaki’s progress in that work, and whether he was
succeeding in the instruction completed to date.  The UDC stated at paragraph
177 of the Decision that “[t]he Appellant did not submit any evidence such as
documentation from the CPSM that could confirmed (sic) his progress to date
particularly related to professionalism”.

[
61
]

The court’s role on the Application is to review the Decision, and the
consideration of new evidence that did not exist at the Hearing is generally irrelevant
to that task.  In my view, the Abner Report is precisely the kind of evidence to
which the rule against admitting extrinsic evidence is designed to apply.  Mr.
Zaki had the opportunity to present independent evidence to the UDC of his
progress with remediation instruction at the Hearing, but he did not file an
interim report or call Dr. Abner as a witness.

[
62
]

Mr. Zaki also raised the criteria set out in
Palmer

v.
The Queen
,
1979 CanLII 8 (SCC)
, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, in support of his request to admit
the Abner Report as evidence.  Mr. Zaki acknowledged that these criteria do not
apply directly in this matter, but he argued that there are overriding
interests of justice considerations that should apply.

[
63
]

The University argued that the
Palmer
criteria arise
from the application of the
Criminal Code
, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46,
and do not apply to judicial review applications.

[
64
]

I agree with the parties that the
Palmer
criteria do
not apply in this case, and I note that even if they did apply, Mr. Zaki has
not satisfied the first criteria, because he has not advanced evidence that the
Abner Report could not have been adduced before the UDC by due diligence.  On
the contrary, it is unclear why Mr. Zaki did not complete all of the sessions
with Dr. Abner and obtain her report before the Hearing.

Conclusion

[
65
]

The Abner Report and all references thereto shall be expunged from
Affidavit #1, without leave to amend, including:

a)

the last two sentences of paragraph 69;

b)

paragraphs 70, 71 and 72; and

c)

Exhibit “D”.

Issue 3:    Should any other paragraphs of Affidavit #1 be
expunged as irrelevant, duplicative or argumentative?

[
66
]

The University seeks to expunge from Affidavit #1 paragraphs 10 – 68,
74 – 75, 96 – 97 and 100 on the basis that they do not contain background
information that is intended to provide additional context to assist the court
with understanding the record.

[
67
]

The University argued that Affidavit #1 contains evidence with
“spin, advocacy, opinion, speculation, and argument”, in the sense that it
includes a special point of view, emphasis, or interpretation presented for the
purpose of influencing opinion, which is improper, and is “directed at the
merits of the matter”, which is inadmissible under
Manitoba Metis
Federation Inc.

[
68
]

The University acknowledged that some of Affidavit #1 contains a
duplicative recitation of the written record before the UDC, but argued that
these sections cannot reasonably be separated from the balance of the evidence,
such that all of the impugned paragraphs should be expunged.

[
69
]

Mr. Zaki argued that this evidence is relevant to his state of mind,
including how he responded to the University in the initial discipline process,
his reasons for making the Recording, and interactions that he had with
University representatives and other individuals, including patients.

The Law

[
70
]

In
Manitoba Metis Federation Inc.
, the court stated
that “the context and background exception is designed to assist the reviewing
court in understanding the record before it”.  An example is where a party
files “an affidavit summarizing, identifying, and highlighting (without
argument) the key documents for the reviewing court’s understanding of the
record”.

Analysis

[
71
]

Paragraphs 10 – 16 of Affidavit #1 pertain to Mr. Zaki’s background,
including his ethnicity and religious beliefs.  None of this evidence falls
within the exceptions to the rule against admitting extrinsic evidence, and some
of it is duplicative of the record before the UDC, such that it is unnecessary.

[
72
]

Paragraphs 17 – 20 of Affidavit #1 relate to the Postings.  Again,
this evidence does not fall within any recognized exception to the rule against
admitting extrinsic evidence, and it is duplicative and unnecessary.

[
73
]

Paragraphs 21 – 64 of Affidavit #1 relate to the investigation that
occurred after the Postings, the remediation process that unfolded, how Mr.
Zaki felt about certain events, and what certain documents reflect.  This
evidence is not admissible under any recognized exception, and parts of it are
duplicative and unnecessary.  In addition, some of these paragraphs contain advocacy
and argument.

[
74
]

Paragraph 65 of Affidavit #1 relates to the appeal of the first
expulsion decision, and paragraphs 66 – 68 relate to the decision of Champagne
J., and events that followed his decision.  Again, the majority of this
evidence is not admissible under any exception, and is duplicative and
unnecessary.

[
75
]

Paragraphs 74 and 75 of Affidavit #1 will remain on the court
record. Both of those paragraphs contain evidence of Mr. Zaki’s observations at
the Hearing, and it is not plain and obvious that they ought to be expunged.
In addition, this evidence will fill a gap in the court record and appear to be
relevant and necessary.  I note Mr. Zaki’s statement that the Dean “appeared to
be angry” at the Hearing is opinion evidence, but the appearance of a person’s
demeanour is a subject that may be opined upon by non-expert witnesses, such
that the statement is admissible.

[
76
]

Paragraphs 96, 97, and 100 of Affidavit #1 reflect evidence that is
irrelevant to the Application, some of which is editorial commentary, and none
of it falls within the exceptions to the rule against admitting extrinsic
evidence.

Conclusion

[
77
]

The following excerpts of Affidavit #1 are expunged, without leave
to amend:

a)

paragraphs 10 – 68; and

b)

paragraphs 96, 97, and 100.

Issue 4:    Should the Notice of Application be Amended?

[
78
]

As set out above, Mr. Zaki seeks to amend the Application to include
specific allegations of bias arising from the relationship between the Chair of
the UDC and the Dean.  Since the Application as filed reflects a request for a
declaration that the Decision was made with a reasonable apprehension of bias,
Mr. Zaki is now seeking to further particularize those allegations on the basis
of information of which he learned, he says, earlier this year.

[
79
]

I will consider the proposed amendments together with the motion to
expunge the balance of Affidavit #2, which contains the evidence filed to
support the amendment.  The following background information is relevant to a
determination of these issues.

[
80
]

The Decision reflects that Mr. Zaki was advised of the identity of
the Chair on August 27, 2021, and that no objections were raised.

[
81
]

The University’s written Student Discipline Appeal Procedure
provides:

2.67    The
Appellant … [has] the right to challenge for cause any member of the UDC
hearing panel … . Such cause may include … bias, or any other factor likely to
prejudice a fair hearing.

[
82
]

The parties agree that at the Hearing, Mr. Zaki raised the matter of
potential bias of the UDC.  The Decision reflects as follows:

[14]    The Appellant and the Respondent can
challenge for cause any member of a UDC Panel.  At the beginning of the hearing
on April 8, 2022, the Appellant raised the matter of potential bias of the UDC
Panel members and asked to question the UDC Panel members on three points that
may influence their decision: (1) conflicting loyalty with either party, (2)
preformed views on the issues in this case, and (3) prior involvement with TDS,
the University’s external counsel, for the judicial review.

[15]    The Respondent was given an
opportunity to respond.  The Respondent submitted that it is a new panel that understands
their duty to disclose any conflicts of interest or bias.  The Respondent
submitted that TDS represented the College during the judicial review, not the
UDC.

[16]    The UDC
Panel did not submit to being questioned by the Appellant, but consistent with
Student
Discipline Appeal Procedure
, it adjourned to consider the challenge and
specifically the three questions raised by the Appellant.  Each member of the
UDC Panel confirmed that there were no reasons to recuse themselves from the
hearing on the grounds of conflict of interest or bias and advised the
parties.  The Chair noted and conveyed to both parties that she is a professor
in the College of Pharmacy and reports to the Dean of Pharmacy.  No objections
were made to her participation in this appeal when the parties were first
advised on August 27, 2021 or at the hearing.

[
83
]

In other words, at the Hearing Mr. Zaki raised potential bias as an
issue generally, but did not raise the specific allegation of bias due to the
working relationship between the Chair and the Dean on which he now seeks to
rely.

The Law

[
84
]

In
AOV Adults Only Video Ltd. v. Manitoba Labour Board
,

2003 MBCA 81
, the court stated that evidence of bias may not be on the record
that would otherwise underlie a judicial review application, such that
additional evidence may be brought forward if it is otherwise admissible.

[
85
]

In
Bernard
, the court stated:

26      I note
parenthetically that if the evidence of natural justice, procedural fairness,
improper purpose or fraud were available at the time of the administrative
proceedings, the aggrieved party would have to object and adduce the evidence
supporting the objection before the administrative decision-maker. Where the
party could reasonably be taken to have had the capacity to object before the
administrative decision-maker and does not do so, the objection cannot be made later
on judicial review:
Zündel v. Canada (Human Rights Commission)
(2000),

2000 CanLII 16575 (FCA)
, 195 D.L.R. (4th) 399, 264 N.R. 174 (Fed. C.A.);
E.C.W.U., Local
916 v. Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 5528 (FCA)
, [1986] 1 F.C. 103 (Fed.
C.A.).

…

35      The
evidence the applicant seeks to introduce in the impugned paragraphs and
exhibits was actually or reasonably available to her with some diligence at the
time of the Board's decision. It was relevant to the Board's consideration of
the merits before it, namely whether the 2008 decision was vitiated by bias or
a failure of natural justice. The evidence in the impugned paragraphs and
exhibits should have been placed before the Board as the merits-decider, not
before this Court as reviewer.

36
It follows that the impugned paragraphs and
exhibits should not be placed before the Court. In this application for
judicial review, they are inadmissible.

[
86
]

In addition, as set out above, in
Hennessey
, the court
stated that a party must object when it is aware of a procedural problem in the
first-instance forum, and give the decision-maker a chance to address the
matter before any harm is done.

[
87
]

Court of King’s Bench Rule 38.05.1(2) provides that the court may
grant leave to amend an application at any stage of the proceeding, on such
terms as are just, unless prejudice would result that could not be compensated
by costs or an adjournment.

[
88
]

The law
[8]

is clear that on a motion for an amendment, the court should consider:

a)

the seriousness of prejudice to the other party;

b)

whether any resulting prejudice could be
compensated for by costs or an adjournment;

c)

whether the moving party delayed, and if so
whether they have explained the delay satisfactorily; and

d)

the nature of the proposed amendment and whether
it raises a valid, arguable point that has merit.  More particularly, the court
should ask whether it is plain and obvious that the proposed amendment has no
reasonable prospect of success.

Analysis

[
89
]

I will consider first the evidentiary issue.

[
90
]

In Affidavit #2, Mr. Zaki deposed that “[a]t the time, I did not
know that the Dean of the College of Pharmacy, like the Associate Dean of the
College of Medicine … reports to [the Dean], who oversees both Colleges as part
of his role as Dean of the Faculty of Health Sciences”.

[
91
]

Mr. Zaki has attached to Affidavit #2 a variety of documents and
policies describing the structure of the Faculty of Health Sciences and the
Colleges of Pharmacy and Medicine, including documents that he submits describe
the powers of the Dean over other positions, including that of the Chair.  I
will make no comment upon the strength of this evidence at this stage,
particularly given that the University has not filed responding evidence, but I
will note that the nature of this allegation requires that it be taken
seriously.

[
92
]

It is clear that evidence of the working relationship between the
Chair and the Dean was not on the record before the UDC, and does not otherwise
underlie the Application.  The question, therefore, is whether the evidence is
otherwise admissible.

[
93
]

There appears to be no question that Mr. Zaki gave notice to the
University in his written submissions that he intended to exercise his right to
ensure that the UDC was independent, and that he did so at the Hearing.  Having
said that, Mr. Zaki did not raise specifically the allegation that the Chair
reported to the Dean through an intermediary.  I accept that at the Hearing Mr.
Zaki was not aware of that alleged relationship, because if he knew about it his
counsel would have raised it.  Similarly, if Mr. Zaki was aware of the alleged relationship
when the Application was filed, he would have particularized the allegations of
bias at that time.  I am also satisfied that once Mr. Zaki learned of the alleged
relationship, he raised it as an issue promptly.

[
94
]

The University submitted, quite rightly, that the court must
consider what information was reasonably available to Mr. Zaki at the Hearing.
Clearly, Mr. Zaki was aware of the Chair’s identity and position months
before the Hearing, and was alive to potential issues of bias at the outset of
the Hearing.  In addition, the documents upon which Mr. Zaki now seeks to rely
were available publicly in advance of the Hearing, with one specific exception
relative to a policy that was updated in early 2024.

[
95
]

Mr. Zaki argued that finding the relevant information equated to a finding
a “needle in a haystack”, but he has not explained how he failed to locate the
information prior to the Hearing, particularly in the context of his concerns
about bias in advance of the proceedings.  He stated in Affidavit #2 that
“…earlier this year, while reviewing documentation from the University website,
I realized that both the College of Medicine and the College of Pharmacy are
underneath the oversight of the Dean …”.

[
96
]

The fact that Mr. Zaki was able to ascertain the alleged reporting
relationship between the Chair and the Dean earlier this year using information
that was available before the Hearing is not supportive of the admission of the
balance of Affidavit #2 on to the evidentiary record on the Application.  As
stated in
Bernard
, extrinsic evidence is not admissible if it was
actually or reasonably available with some diligence.  Mr. Zaki certainly had
adequate time within which to do so, and the necessary information was
available publicly.

[
97
]

Having said that, the problem that I have with expunging the balance
of Affidavit #2 is that Mr. Zaki
did
raise the issue of potential
bias at the outset of the Hearing.  The UDC consulted in camera, after which it
concluded that although the Chair was a member of the College of Pharmacy, no
conflict existed based upon her reporting structure within the College.  The
reasons for the UDC’s decision on this issue are unknown, but Mr. Zaki appears
to have accepted and relied upon that conclusion in good faith.  The Decision reflects
that the UDC understood its duty to disclose any conflicts of interest or bias,
but if the allegations that Mr. Zaki has now made are accurate, and there could
have been a reasonable apprehension of bias at the Hearing that was not
disclosed by the UDC when questioned about potential conflicts, there may be an
impact upon the Application.  In this context, I cannot conclude that it is
plain and obvious that the balance of Affidavit #2 ought to be expunged.

[
98
]

I have considered also the motion to amend the Application.

[
99
]

As set out above, I must consider the seriousness of prejudice to
the University, and whether any prejudice could be compensated for by costs or
an adjournment.  I note that the Application as filed reflects an allegation of
reasonable apprehension of bias, although the basis for that allegation is not
particularized.  In addition, for what appears to be a variety of different
reasons, the Application, filed in August 2022, remains in the early stages of
the process, in that no cross-examinations have yet been conducted and no
substantive briefs filed.  As such, there is no prejudice to the University if
the amendments are allowed at this stage.

[
100
]

I have considered also whether Mr. Zaki delayed his request to amend
the Application, and if so, whether he explained the delay.  The University
submitted that Mr. Zaki could have raised this issue before the UDC, and that
he has failed to explain his delay.  I acknowledge that these types of issues
should be raised as quickly as possible, but I have accepted that Mr. Zaki was
unaware of the relationship between the respective roles of the Chair and the
Dean until earlier this year.  After he became aware of the relationship that
he now alleges, he moved quickly to seek to amend the Application.

[
101
]

Last, I have considered the potential merits of the proposed
amendments, and I cannot conclude that it is plain and obvious that the
proposed amendment has no reasonable prospect of success.  I am mindful of the
fact that although there is no responding evidence before me from the
University regarding the relationship between the positions of the Chair and
the Dean, the University does not accept Mr. Zaki’s allegations.  Having said
that, the record reflects that the Dean was involved in Mr. Zaki’s
expulsion, and that he was a point of contact representing the University,
including in correspondence with the UDC
[9]
.
In addition, it is clear that the Chair and the Dean as faculty members of the
University have some form of working relationship.

[
102
]

I have concluded, therefore, that Mr. Zaki should have the
opportunity to pursue the allegation that there was a reasonable apprehension
of bias at the Hearing given the respective positions of the Chair and the
Dean, and that this question should be explored on the merits of the
Application.

Conclusion

[
103
]

The motion to expunge the balance of Affidavit #2 is dismissed.

[
104
]

The motion to amend the Application is granted.

Issue 5:    Should the Requested Third Party Records be
Disclosed?

[
105
]

Mr. Zaki filed Affidavit #3 in support of his request for the
disclosure of third party records.  More specifically, Mr. Zaki seeks the
disclosure of two disciplinary decisions (the “Disciplinary Decisions”)
involving a student (the “Student”) in the College of Nursing, which is also
part of the Faculty of Health Sciences.  The Student was also suspended for
online posts, but the suspension was overturned by the Local Discipline Committee
(the “LDC”)
[10]

and the Student was returned to the University, despite the fact that they were
apparently unapologetic for their actions.

[
106
]

At my direction, on each of May 13 and May 22, 2024, Mr. Zaki’s
counsel contacted the lawyer who appeared for the Student at their University
disciplinary proceedings via telephone and e-mail.  Counsel did not respond.  On
June 4, 2024, Mr. Zaki served the Student personally with notice of the
third party disclosure request.  Despite these efforts, neither the Student nor
their counsel contacted counsel or the parties in this matter prior to the
hearing before me.

[
107
]

The University argued that there would be risk in disclosing the
Student’s records not having heard from them prior to the hearing.

[
108
]

I concluded that given personal service on the Student, and multiple
attempts at contacting their counsel, I was satisfied that appropriate procedural
steps were taken.  A non-party to litigation cannot be forced to respond, and a
matter may have to proceed in their absence.  Accordingly, I ordered that Mr.
Zaki’s third party disclosure motion would be heard.

[
109
]

Mr. Zaki submitted that the Disciplinary Decisions are relevant to
the Application because:

a)

the reasoning of the LDC will “shed light” on
the importance of academic freedom and freedom of expression to the Faculty of
Health Sciences and the “range of views that it can tolerate being expressed by
its students”; and

b)

the differential treatment of the other student as
compared with Mr. Zaki will support his allegations of bias.

[
110
]

Mr. Zaki submitted that the Disciplinary Decisions can be admitted
as extrinsic evidence to support his allegations of bias.  In addition, if the
motion is granted, appropriate privacy restrictions should be ordered, such as
a sealing order, or appropriate redactions.  Alternatively, Mr. Zaki suggested
that the Disciplinary Decisions be produced for my review.

[
111
]

The University submitted that the Disciplinary Decisions are not
relevant to the Application, and that it must maintain confidentiality in
matters of student discipline pursuant to its by-laws and
The
Freedom of
Information and Protection of Privacy Act
, C.C.S.M. c. F175.

The Law

[
112
]

It is clear that I have jurisdiction to order the production of
relevant documents on a judicial review application (
Jewish Community
Campus of Winnipeg Inc. v. Metaser et al.
,
2013 MBQB 303
).

Analysis

[
113
]

The Disciplinary Decisions post-date the Hearing, and as such are
generally inadmissible.  Although there may be some general similarities
between the Student’s conduct and Mr. Zaki’s conduct, in that both individuals
made controversial postings online, I am not satisfied that the Disciplinary
Decisions are relevant to the Application.  The fact that another Student was
reinstated after making social media posts that were determined to be
antisemitic, discriminatory, and unprofessional, and for which she did not
apologize, will not assist the court in determining the Application, including whether
the UDC was biased against Mr. Zaki.  If that was the law, any two factually similar
cases that were decided differently, by different tribunals within the same
institution, would necessarily apply to one another.  I cannot conceive of how
the Disciplinary Decisions could have any probative value to the Application,
and accordingly Mr. Zaki’s motion for third party disclosure is dismissed.

[
114
]

Mr. Zaki agreed that if the disclosure motion was denied, Affidavit
#3 should be expunged. I have also considered the expungement of Affidavit #3,
and I agree that it is plain and obvious that it should be expunged in its
entirety.

Conclusion

[
115
]

The motion for the disclosure of the Disciplinary Decisions is
dismissed.

[
116
]

Affidavit #3 is expunged.

Conclusion

[
117
]

The University’s motion to expunge is granted, in part.

[
118
]

Mr. Zaki’s motion to amend the Application is granted.

[
119
]

Mr. Zaki’s motion for the disclosure of third party records is
dismissed.

[
120
]

If costs cannot be agreed upon, counsel may seek an appearance to
make submissions.
